summary:
We built a single-player space station operations game, made with the Godot engine and playable in a web browser. You are the only technician on a crewed station in low Earth orbit and must keep the astronaut alive and the station running for a seven-day mission.

The game turns mission design into decisions the player feels. Every system needs power, spare parts and crew time: the oxygen generator, the CO2 scrubber, water recovery, solar arrays, batteries and the cooling loop all wear out and can fail. Orbital eclipses cut solar power every 90 minutes, debris forces evasive burns that cost fuel, and the crew still has to eat, drink, exercise and sleep. Mission Control radios forecasts and advice, and an end-of-mission debrief explains each incident as cause, effect and what to do next time.

It matters because the player learns by doing why life support, power and thermal margins drive real mission planning, and why prevention costs less than repair.
details:
What it does

You play the only technician on a crewed space station in low Earth orbit. The goal is to keep the astronaut healthy and the station working until the end of a seven-day mission. You walk through six modules (living quarters, lab, node, gym, storage and tech bay), use the machines in each one, and decide how to spend your limited time, power, water and spare parts.

How it works

The game runs a simulation of the station in five-minute steps:
- Air: an oxygen generator and a CO2 scrubber keep each module breathable. The scrubber saturates and must be regenerated.
- Water: a recovery system turns waste water back into clean water. Its filter gets dirty and its motor can burn out.
- Power: solar arrays charge a battery. The station passes into Earth's shadow on every 90-minute orbit, so the battery has to carry the load. When power runs short, the station sheds less important equipment first.
- Heat: equipment and crew produce heat that a coolant loop and radiator must remove.
- Crew: the astronaut needs meals, water, toilet breaks, two hours of exercise a day and a full night of sleep. Skipping them lowers health and slows work.
- Wear: every machine loses health as it runs and can fail. Servicing it early with a spare part is cheaper than repairing it after it breaks.
- Hazards: debris on the flight path forces an evasive burn that costs fuel.

Mission Control sends radio forecasts and advice. Yellow and red alerts point to the room and machine that need attention. A morning report summarizes the night, and the end screen lists each incident as cause, effect and a suggestion.

Benefits and intended impact

The game is for students and anyone curious about how a space mission is kept alive day to day. Players learn by doing why CO2 is a more urgent problem than oxygen, why an eclipse drains the battery, why every burn costs fuel, and why maintenance decides whether a mission succeeds. We want players to finish a run able to explain those ideas in their own words.

What makes it creative

Most space games are about flying. Ours is about operations: the unglamorous work that real missions depend on. The pressure comes from small problems that pile up when they are put off, not from random disasters. We also set fairness rules for ourselves: every problem gives a warning, can be detected, can be prevented and can be recovered from, and the debrief always explains why it happened.

Factors we considered

- Correct concepts: every physical idea shown must be right, even where the mechanics are simplified.
- Plausible numbers: values are kept in a realistic order of magnitude, and scaled only where the game needs it.
- Repeatable runs: all randomness comes from a seed, so a run can be replayed and tested.
- Accessibility: subtitles, reduced motion, high contrast and text size settings, and a how-to-play guide for new players.
- Web delivery: the game uses a renderer that can be exported to the browser.

Tools

Godot Engine 4.7.2 and GDScript for the game; JSON files for all balance numbers, text and content; Python for a sprite tool; headless automated tests for the simulation and every screen; Git and GitHub for teamwork. Planet visuals use the open-source Pixel Planets shaders by Deep-Fold (MIT licence). AI coding assistants helped write and review code.
